# Library API and init State Decision Record

## 2023-06-23: An Entry Left by a Test File

This page was not originally organized around API names. The question that needed answering was: after a library call completes, can the directory value held by the caller be used directly to continue reading the generated project? The easiest place to retrace the action is `tests/integration/helpers/project.rs`. It connects both to the generation call and to path and file reads, making it an entry point for reproducing the behavior, but that does not make it the owner of the generation implementation.

The written notes at the time contained only a few lines of adjacency information:

```rust
use assert_cmd::prelude::*;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Read;
use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};
```

The extended note for `assert_cmd` indicates that auxiliary assertions may be connected to command invocations; `File` and `Read` indicate that file reads occur; and `Path` and `PathBuf` indicate that paths are passed or compared. They can help the next person start investigating from a local action, but a type name alone cannot determine whether a value is the template source, a parent directory, a temporary location, or the final project directory. For that reason, the early editor did not turn the test helper file into an implementation index.

The first candidate was the path temporarily stored while processing the template source. It seemed reasonable because the path value might be moved around before and after generation, and returning it appeared to avoid one extra computation. The second candidate was the already-created target directory for the caller to continue opening files. This candidate was closer to what the caller did with the returned value, but at the time it was still unclear whether file expansion and initialization had completed.

That day, the second candidate was first recorded as a working hypothesis. It only determined where to look first in the next round; it was not the finalized API wording. The pre-call cwd, the supplied target location, the function's return object, the files in the generated tree, and the state observed by the hook were recorded in separate columns; if these were initially collapsed into “the path is correct,” it would later be difficult to tell which specific item had actually been observed.

## The Review Did Not Accept the Statement “The Directory Exists”

A few days later, the review broke down a seemingly passing scenario. The appearance of a directory in the file system only shows that the name exists. It does not show that the returned object is the project directory, that the template file the caller will read later has been written, or that the hook saw the initialized state.

The review notes did not provide a complete implementation path; they only changed how the verification was laid out: first save the pre-call cwd and target location; after the call completes, directly inspect where the returned object points; then find the file to be read in the actual generated tree; finally, observe the hook state separately. Here, “directly” means not looking for the file again from another familiar directory; it does not mean adding a new parameter to the library call.

Counterexample one is directory offset. The return value may point to a real, existing directory, while the project file the caller needs is in its parent directory or adjacent to it. An existence assertion alone hides this difference. Counterexample two is the opposite: a template file can be read from a known location, but the return value does not point to that location. Looking only at file readability misses the problem with the returned object.

The two counterexamples cannot both be recorded simply as “generation failed.” The first is primarily a mismatch between the return location and the project location; the second is primarily that the read location has not been linked to the returned object. They may occur at the same time, but during remediation we need to know which one was observed first. The review did not require deriving this relationship from the name of `PathBuf`; the relationship must be examined in the generated file tree.

## Provisional wording left from 2023

The decision made during this period was small: continue treating the target directory as a candidate return object, and keep a separate set of records for observing init. No decision was made about all hook fields, no decision was made that one particular directory layout would apply to all callers, and the import at the top of the test file was not treated as proof of ordering during the generation stage.

The field table used at the time was roughly as follows:

| Observation point | Recorded content | Question it could answer at the time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before the call | cwd, target location | Where does the relative path start? |
| After the return | Location pointed to by the returned object | Which path value did API hand over? |
| Generated tree | Whether the target file could be opened | Is the project file readable yet? |
| Hook side | Observable init state | Which stage did the hook observe? |

This table did not appear in the early files; it was added as a work breakdown on a sticky note after the review. It was not a long-term acceptance checklist either. For example, the target location and the returned object may look similar as strings, but we still need to check whether they fall within the same actual project directory; even if the file can be opened, we still need to retain the path used to open it.

A shortcut was also discussed at the time: have each caller rederive the project path from the parameters and target directory, while the library call only hands over some path from the generation process. This would let the library explain one less layer, but different callers would each form their own “completion location.” Once the parent directory, project name, or relative path differs, an offset in the returned object becomes harder to detect. It was not written down as a decision; it was retained only as an option that had been compared.

## 2024-04: Review on the same tree

A subsequent review no longer treated the “known target directory” as a substitute entry point for reading files. The method remained simple: record cwd and the target location before the call, first obtain the return path after the call, then use that return path to go back into the generated tree and find the project file; separately, check which directory actually appeared under the target location; finally, check the hook state on its own.

This review left three scenarios that are easy to conflate. The first is when the directory already exists, but the returned value points to the parent directory or a neighboring location. The second is when the returned value points to the project directory, but the expected files still cannot be read near the return boundary. The third is when the file has appeared, but there is still no separate description of the init state visible to the hook. The wording for all three must not simply say “generation complete,” or the historical record will lose the distinctions.

An older page contains a broader judgment:

> Deprecated: Once the return directory appears, the library call can be considered complete; call Fang Ke to complete the remaining file reads yourself.

This sentence was not removed. It records why directory existence alone was checked at the time, and also explains why early callers put the path location and file writing in the same feedback. The “Deprecated” label added later only limits the period during which this sentence applies; it does not turn it into wording that looks correct today.

The same review also confirmed a narrower boundary: `File` and `Read` support helper code reading files, but do not specify whether the read occurs before or after the hook; `Path` and `PathBuf` support passing, comparison, and returning to the file tree, but do not specify the semantics of the values themselves. This boundary remains in place because reconstructing the generation-stage order directly from the file header would make the old page appear more complete than the evidence available at the time.

## The Two Shortcuts Set Aside

The first shortcut is looking only at the directory. This approach is fast at the start of an investigation, because once the directory appears, the subsequent reads can proceed; the problem is that it does not expose the offset between the returned object and the actual project directory. Later records did not call it entirely useless: it can still serve as an observation point for the file tree appearing, but it cannot serve as the basis for judging the return value.

The second shortcut is reading files only from another known location. It can help confirm that template content does exist somewhere, but it bypasses the path that API passes to the caller. If the return value is wrong while the file location happens to be correct, looking only at the read results produces an overly optimistic conclusion. This is also why the review insisted on retaining the original value of the returned object.

There was also a statement that “the end of the hook is the return boundary.” It is closer to a sequencing issue than “the directory exists, so it is complete,” but it still conflates the init state visible to the hook with the template payload being written to disk. This statement did not become a decision; it remained only at the margins of the old discussion and was later treated as an outdated judgment.

## Review Excerpt and an Unfinished Experiment

The review excerpt from 2024 was brief:

> Do not ask only which Path was returned; put the return value back into the generated file tree.
>
> If the file can be read but the returned directory is the parent directory, report a path issue; do not classify it as template content.
>
> If the directory is correct but the file has not yet been written to disk, the name must not be shared with path errors.

The excerpt did not provide a field list for the hook, nor did it say that the test helper file was the implementation owner. What it actually changed was the observation order and the error categorization.

Once, an experiment left behind only process conclusions and no complete output. The first record treated “path exists” as a success signal; on review, it became clear that existence proved neither that the name was the actual generated project directory nor that the template files had been fully written before return. The second record separately documented the function’s return path, the project files under the target location, and the directory state visible after the hook. It did not expand the test helper file’s responsibilities to cover the generation flow; it only ensured that reads and assertions no longer silently used the known path beside it.

Regarding init, the experiment supports only one conservative approach: inspect the inclusion and exclusion results within the same generated tree, rather than substituting global configuration for the state of this generation. Which states counted as part of init and which were merely ordinary files after expansion were not itemized at the time. This gap was not later filled in by speculation.

## A margin note left by another editor

The margin note had flagged an adjacent issue: if the caller’s cwd changes between before and after the public call, relative-path reads may produce a second kind of discrepancy. Whether cwd remains unchanged and which directory is returned are not the same assertion. An unchanged cwd cannot, in turn, prove that the returned path is correct; a changed cwd cannot, by itself, prove that the project files were not written to disk.

The same margin note also asked who provides the parent directory. In the test helper file, verification can start from the target location, but the existing material does not list all parameter forms, nor does it generalize any particular test directory tree into a constraint for all calls. This question remains near this page; it was not folded into path determination.

Another question mark concerned whether the init state seen by the hook includes initialization metadata or refers only to ordinary files visible in the generated tree. Existing records support only “check inclusion and exclusion in the same tree”; they do not support a complete enumeration. There was also a question mark about timing across different entry points: whether the command-line entry point, library call, and test helper entry point share the same return boundary. The old page did not retain enough of the implementation relationships.

## 2025-08: Later-added criteria

The latest consolidation placed three objects side by side near the return boundary: the object returned by the public call, the payload in the actual generated project directory, and the init state observable by the hook. They may occur consecutively within one call, but must not replace one another when making judgments. The reviewer first retains the cwd from before the call; after return, uses the returned path to get back to the project tree; when init needs to be checked, still observes inclusion and exclusion in that tree.

The public Rust call generate(GenerateArgs) must return Result<PathBuf>; on success, PathBuf is the actual generated project directory, and the payload has been written to disk before return. The acceptance record uses generate returned the wrong path and generate did not create the project payload to distinguish the return-value issue from the disk-write issue.

This convention only addresses the local relationships among the returned object, the project directory, and writing to disk before returning. It does not name all public fields for the hook, nor does it elevate `tests/integration/helpers/project.rs` into a description of the generation implementation. If reproduction fails, first compare the returned `PathBuf` with the actual generated project directory, then check whether the payload exists before returning; only after both checks line up should you continue to examine the init state visible to the hook.

An easily confused ordering note is still retained here: the observation order is not the internal state machine reconstructed from the test helper files. Its sole purpose is to establish a correspondence between the return value and the file tree first. The hook's state is another observation point; the fact that it is examined last does not mean this page establishes the complete internal sequence.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> BeforeCall
    BeforeCall --> GeneratedTree
    GeneratedTree --> PayloadWrittenToDisk
    PayloadWrittenToDisk --> HookVisibleInitState
    HookVisibleInitState --> ReturnActualGeneratedDirectory
    ReturnActualGeneratedDirectory --> [*]
```

The arrows in the diagram represent the observation order used on this page, not state transitions proven by the test helper files. In particular, “hook-visible” is only a point of observation during the run, not a new set of field names introduced by this page. The diagram also does not collapse the caller's cwd, the target parent directory, and the file-reading action into a single state; these objects still each have their own place in the review records.

## Appendix of old examples: the shape of early assertions

### Example one: seeing the directory first

The old example first confirmed that a directory existed, then read a file from another known location. When both actions passed, the record described the result as “generation complete”. It was later discovered that this arrangement only proved that the two locations each met their respective checks, not that the return value and the read location were the same. It is retained in the appendix as an example of the old assertion order, not as verbatim steps for today.

### Example two: the file can be opened

Another old example recorded only a successful file read, without printing the returned path. It can show that a file exists at some location, but cannot show that the `PathBuf` provided by API points to that location. The later column layout therefore separated “the file can be read” from “the returned object is correct”. The old record contains no further run results, so the appendix stops here.

### Example three: three things squeezed into one line

Another line described the appearance of the target directory, the unpacking of files, and the hook-visible state as the same “completion”. The line is very short, but does not show exactly which step was observed or whether the files came from the returned path. It was not deleted; a note was simply left beside the old example: brevity does not mean that the three observations have already substantiated one another.

### Example four: inferring the return value from the target location

Early reviews sometimes read files from a target location already at hand, then treated the successful read as proof that the returned path was correct. This approach was retained because it could quickly determine whether generated content existed somewhere; its drawback is equally clear: the return value never entered the assertion. If only file writing was fixed later, a path mismatch could still remain in the result.

## Verification entry points and remaining items not yet separated out

When entering via `tests/integration/helpers/project.rs`, you can first look at the direct use of `generate` and `PathBuf`, and then at the read operations related to `File` and `Read`. The imports at the top of the file support these local observations, but cannot replace a complete description of the generated implementation. The cwd before and after the call, the returned path, the payload in the target directory, and the hook-visible state are still recorded separately.

This page also does not consolidate the adjacent parent-directory parameters, cwd changes, and timing across different entry points into a new decision. They are adjacent to the path issue, but each requires different evidence from the actual environment. If only one of them is confirmed next time, update only that item on the old page; do not fill in the relationships that have not yet been observed as a complete flow.

Finally, retain the early working hypothesis, the review breakdown, the experiments whose complete output was not saved, the overturned old sentences, the shortcuts that were not adopted, and the wording added later. The appendix's “the directory appearing means completion” still belongs to an early judgment; it explains the history, but cannot once again serve as the basis for conclusions about return values or files being written to disk.

# VCS Precedence and Rhai Helper Proposal

This round looks at template declarations and caller choices as parts of the same problem. Parameter definitions for the generation entry point are concentrated in `src/args.rs`; the file shows `StructOpt`, `crate::git`, and direct dependencies for error handling, but the entry point's location alone does not establish which layer ultimately performs initialization.

There are two candidate approaches: the template provides a default initialization method that callers can override when needed, or the template declaration always takes precedence over the caller. The former preserves template conventions while letting callers adapt to existing directories; the latter produces more predictable results, but would give a generation request hidden repository side effects. The first draft favors the former. We still need to confirm whether “disable initialization” is a normal override value or a separate branch.

Case-conversion helpers are another part of the interface. Template authors want to turn display names into forms suitable for variables and filenames; word-splitting rules should not be hidden in templates. We need to retain an entry point on the Rhai side and find a name containing an acronym as a sample, to avoid splitting consecutive uppercase letters into multiple words.

No changes to the tag and template-test entry points at this stage. This proposal only covers the behavior boundaries for initialization choices and conversion helpers.

# VCS Precedence and Rhai Helper Proposal

After review, the issue isn't just “which value overrides which.” The template declaration describes the initial environment the template expects, while the command-line arguments describe this generation request. Both may be present, but they mean different things. Making the template a rule that cannot be overridden would prevent callers from reusing the same template in existing directories, directories without a repository, or external initialization workflows.

The argument side uses `--vcs`. The template side already has configuration locations such as `[template] vcs`, so the proposal is to interpret the template value as a default rather than a second required parameter. Template authors can still express their usual initialization approach, and callers don't have to edit the template file to change the result of a single generation request.

This review did not support another compromise: allowing callers to change the template value to Git, but not to turn off initialization. That compromise appears to preserve the template's expectations, but it still hides assumptions about directory structure and subsequent hooks in the template. If the caller explicitly requests no initialization, generation should follow that choice through to completion, rather than creating a repository first and then trying to clean it up.

The previous draft treated “disable initialization” as a separate branch. That needs to be corrected to make it part of the normal precedence rules. However, the point at which `.git` is created still needs to be checked in the implementation. The argument-parsing file can help locate the input structure; it is not a substitute for checking the generation flow.

The Rhai test sample is set to `Hello HTTP World`. The goal is for the helper to produce `hello_http_world`: HTTP should remain a single word, rather than becoming `h_t_t_p`. This also defines the helper's scope: it handles name conversion, not project name normalization or crate name derivation.

Still unresolved: whether template hooks read the state after initialization, and whether there is a dedicated error or skip path when initialization is disabled. This needs to be confirmed in the generation path; this page does not infer hook execution order from it.

# VCS Precedence and Rhai Helper Proposal

The interface changes were first discussed in terms of template defaults, but we later found that caller needs were easier to overlook: the same template may be used for a new directory or with a target location prepared by an external workflow. If a template declaration directly mandates an action, callers can only modify the template or accept a repository initialization they don't need. That cost should not fall on the template, nor should implicit cleanup hide it.

`src/args.rs` remains the entry point for looking up the parameter structure. The file introduces `StructOpt` and sits directly alongside `crate::git`; this is enough to show that the parameters and Git-related paths need to be reviewed together. It does not establish the full relationship between template configuration and execution paths, so this proposal defines semantics only for the exposed choices, without treating the arrangement of implementation files as a conclusion.

An early draft separated three cases: the template requests initialization, the caller requests initialization, and the caller requests that initialization be disabled. That wording made the last case look like an exception, and reviewers could easily read it as “the template takes precedence unless handled otherwise.” That wording has been discarded. Disabling initialization is not a corrective action; it is an explicit generation choice.

The decision is: when the caller does not pass --vcs, [template] vcs supplies the default for repository initialization; an explicit --vcs always takes precedence, and .git must not be created when the final choice is None.

This rule separates the sources into two layers. The template supplies only a default, allowing its usual environment to be recorded in configuration; caller parameters apply only to this generation run, allowing callers to use their own version control arrangements. When neither layer is present, retain the generator's existing default handling rather than introducing a third configuration source in this proposal.

None must hold true for the output directory, not merely mean that an initialization command is skipped. If the generation path writes Git metadata and then deletes it, hooks, error recovery, and directory checks may all observe that intermediate state; this is inconsistent with the caller's choice not to initialize. Implementation checks should therefore target the final directory and cover the combination where the template supplies a default but the caller explicitly disables initialization. Conversely, when the template makes no declaration and the caller explicitly selects initialization, that should use the same selection entry point rather than maintaining different creation logic for the two sources.

The withdrawal criteria are narrowed accordingly: if the implementation cannot guarantee the absence of `.git` when the final choice is None, do not merge the interface change described as “template defaults, caller Fang Ke overrides.” Fix the timing of initialization first rather than silently downgrading the parameter to a suggestion. The template configuration wording must not continue to describe initialization as mandatory, since that could mislead callers.

The case-conversion helper proceeds alongside this decision but does not share its precedence logic. It is intended for name transformations in Rhai templates. The retained sample is `Hello HTTP World`, with `hello_http_world` as the result; the acronym HTTP is preserved as a single word in the result. This rule covers only this helper's word-splitting result; it does not extend to other normalization processes for project names, target directories, or Cargo crate names.

The implementation should not require template authors to piece together multiple case checks themselves. The Rhai entry point should make this one conversion rule stable, with templates simply consuming the result. This proposal does not need additional special conventions for converting ordinary words; samples containing consecutive uppercase letters already define the boundary of this change.

Two areas of work are not expanded by this decision. First, tag selection and template testing continue to be handled through their respective entry points, without tying them to VCS precedence. Second, whether template hooks can observe initialization state needs to be checked separately in the generation execution path; without evidence, do not make it part of the template contract.

Before merging, retain three categories of regression tests: the template supplies a default and the caller passes no parameter; the caller explicitly overrides the template; and the final choice is None. The first two verify source precedence, while the last verifies that the directory contains no leftover Git metadata. On the Rhai side, only the name sample containing an acronym needs to be retained, to prevent later changes from degrading `hello_http_world` into letter-by-letter splitting.

The old draft treated “disable initialization” as an exceptional branch still to be added; it is now a normal choice. The helper's scope remains unchanged.

# Project identity and template revision troubleshooting tree

First inspect the generated directory name; don't immediately treat it as evidence of the template contents. In some recent samples, the init hook writes back the project name; other samples require fetching content from a particular tag of the Git template. Both actions happen during generation, but the anomaly observed in the field may not come from the same place.

The working hypothesis is that the name obtained during the interactive phase is only the initial input. After the hook writes back a new name, subsequent directory handling and template variables may need to be read again. This hypothesis has not been tied to a specific call site, so it can only guide what to record first.

```text
Generation result is incorrect
├─ Did the hook write the project name?
│  ├─ Not sure
│  │  └─ First record the original input and actual directory; don't attribute it to the hook
│  └─ Confirmed
│     ├─ Directory is still the original input
│     │  └─ Record the write-back value and check whether subsequent steps picked it up
│     └─ Directory has changed
│        └─ Then check whether a project-name variable appears in the template
└─ Content looks like another template revision
   ├─ No identifiable template content
   │  └─ Don't determine whether the wrong tag was selected
   └─ Identifiable content
      └─ Record the selected tag and output separately
```

Earlier records checked only the target directory. That was useful because the directory was visible first, but it left a gap: even if the directory name changed, the project name and crate name in the template may still use the initial input. Don't use “directory changed” as a substitute for checking the rendered output.

You can start by opening `src/template_variables/project_name.rs`. The file header directly depends on `heck::{ToKebabCase, ToSnakeCase}`, so the hyphenated and underscored forms provide adjacent conversion clues here. This cannot show where the init hook executes, nor can import alone establish which value is the final source.

When retrieving a template by tag, first confirm whether the output contains content that distinguishes the revision. If it does not, write only “not yet compared”; don't guess which revision was selected based on the directory name, template address, or whether generation succeeded. A specified tag indicates selection intent; it does not prove that the corresponding content was retrieved.

The conclusion in the old note was: once the hook renames the project and the directory changes accordingly, the project-name check can be closed. Retain this judgment provisionally; later, use a sample where the directory changed but the variables were not checked to decide whether it remains usable.

For the next investigation, capture at least: the original project name, the value written by the hook, the actual directory, the form in which the project name appears in the template, and whether a tag was specified. If the template has no project-name variable, record that as observed; don't fill it in with the result from another generation.

# Project Identity and Template revision Troubleshooting Tree

When generation results are abnormal, first split the notes into two parts: project identity and template revision. Previously, they were written as one continuous workflow, which made it easy during verification to conclude that “the directory is wrong, so the tag is wrong too”. There is not enough evidence for this conclusion: the directory is part of the generation target, while the template revision is part of source selection; both sides may have problems, or only one side may lack observations.

## Start from the Old Entry Point, but Do Not Treat It as the Cause

The earliest investigation started from `src/template_variables/project_name.rs`. The file itself only provides clues around project name format conversion; the following is visible at the top of the file:

```rust
use heck::{ToKebabCase, ToSnakeCase};
```

When you see the directory using hyphens and the crate using underscores, do not immediately record the difference in appearance as a failure. Both forms may derive from the same project identity. The actual issue to investigate here is: after the hook renames the project, are the directory and rendering variables still drawing from different sources?

The old rule was “a changed directory is enough”. This rule is now marked as **obsolete**, but is not deleted. It was once the only result that could be observed consistently; the problem is that it mistook a partial observation for a complete assessment. A directory change only shows that path handling saw some new value; it does not prove that the template variables also stopped using the interactive input at the same time.

## First Preserve a Complete Identity Sample

Do not start by generating repeatedly. The first time you see the hook rename the project, first write the following items in the same record of the observed state:

- The project name entered during the interactive stage;
- The project name after the init hook writes it;
- The actual generated directory;
- `project-name` visible after template rendering;
- `crate_name` visible after template rendering.

If one item is not visible, do not infer it from the others. In particular, when only the directory and crate name are visible, you cannot assert that `project-name` has been updated; the template may not have included it in this output. A blank is neither failure nor success; it only means that this sample did not provide a point of comparison.

```text
Identity branch
│
├─ Cannot confirm that the hook wrote back a name
│  └─ Treat it as a normal generation result for now; do not record it as an identity normalization anomaly
│
├─ The value written back by the hook is the same as the original input
│  └─ This is not a rename sample; keep the record, but do not verify subsequent use after a rename
│
├─ The value written back by the hook is different, but the directory still uses the original input
│  └─ Keep both values and check whether subsequent steps received the written-back value
│
├─ The value written back by the hook is different, the directory has changed, but the variables still resemble the original input
│  └─ Continue comparing the source of each variable; do not explain away the differences as format conversion
│
└─ The value written back by the hook is different, and the directory and all observed variables use the new identity
   └─ End the identity branch for now; the template revision still needs a separate check
```

“The variables still resemble the original input” does not mean that the strings must be exactly identical. The directory, `project-name`, and `crate_name` may use different formats. What needs to be recorded clearly is: which variables can still be traced to the original input, and which variables already reflect the identity written back by the hook. `ToKebabCase` and `ToSnakeCase` can only help locate what is being formatted; they cannot replace this comparison.

## A Verification That Checked Only the Directory

One verification recorded the changed directory as “restored”. Looking back later, that check had not read any project name variables in the template; it had only confirmed the path. It did not prove that the hook had not executed, nor did it find a problem with tag selection; it only showed that the old rule treated a correct directory as an overly strong stopping condition.

After this verification, the recording method was changed to write the original input first, followed by the value after the hook. If the two values are the same, the sample is not treated as a rename case; only if they differ are the directory and visible variables listed side by side, item by item. This avoids substituting a normal generation result for a counterexample involving a hook rename.

Manual records are still kept in the following format. Each field may be blank, but results from another generation run must not be mixed in.

```text
Original project name:
Value written by the hook:
Actual directory:
project-name:
crate_name:
Locations where the original input is still visible:
```

If the directory has changed but there is no place to inspect the template variables, the record should stop at “directory observed, variables not compared”. Do not write “project name fully synchronized”. Conversely, if the template shows only one variable and the directory was not preserved, write only “variable observed, directory not compared”.

## A Separate Sheet for Template revision

When the template content looks like another version, first ask whether `--tag` was explicitly passed in this run. The `--tag` option of `generate` is used to select the content corresponding to a specified tag in a Git template repository. It has no direct bearing on assessing a project directory rename: a correct directory does not imply a correct selection, and a correct selection does not imply that the variables have been updated after the hook.

A revision sample must preserve at least two kinds of information: the selection value, and content in the output that actually distinguishes the template version. Recording only the tag name is not enough; later, it will be impossible to distinguish “the content was not retrieved according to the selection” from “the output content cannot be compared at all”.

```text
Template content does not look like the expected revision
│
├─ --tag was not specified
│  └─ Do not attribute this to tag selection; leave this branch
│
├─ --tag was specified, but the output has no content that distinguishes the revision
│  └─ Stop here; the current sample cannot be used to compare tag content
│
├─ --tag was specified, the output distinguishes the revision, and the content does not match
│  └─ Keep the selection value and corresponding output, and check template source selection
│
└─ --tag was specified, and the output content matches
   └─ End the revision branch; do not use it to explain project name variables
```

Here, “distinguishable” must come from template content that is actually visible after generation. The Git address, generated directory, directory timestamp, and the default branch as remembered by the observer cannot replace it. If the output cannot distinguish the revision, you can write “cannot compare” in the record; do not guess a version just to close the branch.

The old instructions once treated “the tag parameter was supplied” as evidence that the content had been retrieved according to the tag. This practice should also be considered outdated. The option only indicates what the caller wants to select; the output content indicates whether this run's result matches that selection.

## Boundaries Established in Review

The review confirmed that the two troubleshooting tracks can end independently.

The project identity side addresses whether the directory and template variables still use the values from the interactive stage after the hook writes back a value. Here, `project_name.rs` can be used to trace back to the adjacent formatting code, but the file location cannot be used to infer where the hook implementation belongs.

The template revision side addresses whether the final rendered content corresponds to the expected revision after a selection value is specified. Here, output content that distinguishes versions must be preserved; it should not be inferred from the directory name.

Therefore, while the identity branch is still open, the revision branch may still have a definite result; when the revision branch has ended, the identity variables may still be unchecked. When both branches have blanks, preserve the blanks separately; do not combine them into “template anomaly”.

## Local Areas Still to Investigate

- The connection between format conversion in `project_name.rs` and reading the value again after the hook still needs to be confirmed by following the actual references;
- The order of tag selection and template root determination has not yet been established in this record;
- If the hook rename affects only the directory and not the rendering variables, preserve the complete sample rather than explaining it away as a difference between hyphens and underscores;
- If the output has no content that distinguishes the revision, the revision branch can only remain in the not-compared state.

The old directory check is still retained above so that people arriving through old links can understand why only path results were recorded previously. Troubleshooting now starts with two records: one comparing project identity, and one comparing template content.

# Project Identity and Template revision Troubleshooting Tree

The generated directory had been renamed, but the original input was still visible in the template. This was the earliest observation recorded on this page. Later, checks of Git templates fetched by tag were recorded in the same batch of generation records, so “wrong directory,” “wrong variables,” and “wrong template version” were, for a time, written up as the same kind of issue. The old entry point usually led people to the directory name first, so this page still starts with the directory; but do not now let the directory serve as evidence for template content.

First, separate the symptoms in front of you. Until you confirm that the init hook wrote the project name, do not attribute directory differences to identity normalization; until you confirm that the output contains template content that distinguishes revisions, do not judge whether the wrong tag was selected. Both things can happen in a single generation run, but the result of one cannot be used to draw a conclusion about the other.

```text
Start: Generated output does not match expectations
│
├─ Has the init hook been confirmed to have written the project name
│  ├─ No, or no record
│  │  └─ Do not enter the identity normalization branch; retain only the ordinary directory or rendering observations
│  └─ Yes
│     ├─ The directory is still the original input
│     │  └─ Record the original value and the written-back value, and check whether subsequent steps receive the written-back value
│     ├─ The directory has changed, but template variables still point to the original input
│     │  └─ Continue checking identity recomputation; do not explain this as a formatting difference
│     └─ Both the directory and visible variables have changed
│        └─ The identity branch can end
│
└─ Does the output contain content that distinguishes template revisions
   ├─ No
   │  └─ Do not judge whether the tag selection is correct
   └─ Yes
      ├─ --tag was not specified
      │  └─ Do not use the tag issue branch
      ├─ The content does not match the specified tag
      │  └─ Record the selected value and the output, and check template source selection
      └─ The content matches the specified tag
         └─ The revision branch can end
```

This tree is not a call graph. It only specifies which value to collect first during investigation, and when to stop because the evidence is insufficient. The directory, template variables, and template content are different aspects to observe; do not mark the other two as normal just because one is already normal.

## 2023-05-24: Initially, Only the Directory Was Checked

The first record was brief: after the hook changed the name, if the target directory changed along with it, the project rename was considered successful. That judgment was understandable at the time. The directory was the easiest object to find after generation, template variables did not consistently appear in every sample, and template content fetched by tag had not yet been included in the same record.

The original wording from the old notes is preserved below:

> When the directory is correct, there is no need to check the project name variables.

This statement is **no longer applicable**. It was once a time-saving check sequence, not a complete identity assessment. A correct directory only shows that path handling used a new value; it does not show that every subsequent variable in the template has moved away from the input entered during the interactive phase.

The initial local navigation was `src/template_variables/project_name.rs`. The file header shows:

```rust
use heck::{ToKebabCase, ToSnakeCase};
```

This fragment makes the directory form and the crate form appear side by side. As a result, the difference between hyphens and underscores is often misread as an anomaly, especially when the generated directory and template variables are compared at the same time. The old records did not distinguish between “different forms” and “different sources,” so whenever one location looked like a reasonable kebab or snake form, it was easy to record that the project names were already consistent.

Only one reliable action can be drawn from this early material: open the format conversion locations related to the project name and record the forms in which the directory and variables each appear. You cannot infer the init hook's execution point from an import, nor can you infer from this path name that all subsequent variables are constructed here.

## Early working hypothesis, preserved without edits

The working hypothesis at the time was: the name obtained during the interactive stage is the default value, and the name written back by the hook mainly affects the target directory. Template variables may continue to use the initial value; as long as the rendered character form has no obvious errors, leave it alone for now.

This hypothesis was later withdrawn, but it is retained here because it explains why old records often contain only a directory name, a note saying “the hook has run,” and incomplete template output. It also explains why some people treated the difference in appearance between `project-name` and `crate_name` as the same problem.

The old hypothesis had two practical limitations.

First, it did not require saving the original input and the value written by the hook. Without these two reference points, an “old name” seen later could be a formatted result or could truly be the previous input; there is no way to distinguish between them.

Second, it did not require preserving the locations where the values appeared in the template. The directory alone cannot tell you whether rendering used the same identity, or whether a variable was absent from the sample altogether.

Therefore, when starting from an old page or an old command record, do not fill in variable values that were not recorded at the time. If the old record lacks template output, acknowledge only that it can show a directory change; do not elevate it into evidence that the entire generation process already uses the new name consistently.

## 2024-04-22: Expand the identity sample to five values

The later review did not start by changing the implementation. Instead, it changed the records to a side-by-side comparison. Whenever confirming that the hook changed the name, first preserve these five items:

- The original project name from the interactive stage;
- The project name after the init hook writes it;
- The actual generated directory;
- The `project-name` that appears after rendering;
- The `crate_name` that appears after rendering.

These values do not have to be character-for-character identical. Directories often need to retain the hyphenated form, while crate names often need the underscored form. When comparing them, the question is whether they are still derived from the same identity, not whether the two formats can be forced into one completely identical text string.

For manual records, continue using the blanks below. This allows some samples to have no visible variables; blanks must be retained, not filled in with results from another generation run.

```text
Original project name:
Hook write:
Actual directory:
project-name:
crate_name:
Location where the original input is still visible:
```

If the value written by the hook is the same as the original input, this record does not constitute a rename case. It can show that the hook path was traversed, but it cannot be used to verify the normalization process after renaming. Only when the two values differ do the directory and variables have a common basis for comparison.

If only the directory and crate name were saved, the record should say “the directory and crate name were observed; project-name was not compared.” If the template only displays `project-name`, it should not be assumed that `crate_name` was synchronized. Omitting one variable from the template output does not indicate an error; it simply means that this run did not provide an observation point for that variable.

## 2024-04-23: Review addendum

The review pointed out that the original linear formulation treated format conversion as source determination. `ToKebabCase` and `ToSnakeCase` show that two conversions are present near the project name, but do not prove that every variable reads from the same input.

The revised conclusion is narrower: correct formatting cannot offset a source mismatch. If the directory already uses the value written by the hook while a variable can still be traced to the original interactive input, the identity branch is not complete; conversely, if a variable looks like the old format, its continued origin from the old input cannot be inferred from the format alone. The original value and the written-back value are still needed as references.

One easy-to-miss stopping condition was also retained: when the original input or hook-written value is unavailable, do not classify a “name mismatch” as a post-hook identity issue. The directory and rendered text can still be recorded, but the conclusion should stop at “identity source not confirmed.” This is closer to the actual evidence than attributing every name difference to `project_name.rs`.

The review did not combine tag selection into this five-item table. The reason is simple: the tag determines the revision of the Git template, while project identity determines the subsequent use of the generated path and variables. Both tracks may need to be checked at the same time, but they require different outputs.

## A failed directory recheck

There was once a recheck that examined only the generated directory. Because the directory was already in the form visible after the hook write, the record was marked “restored.” In retrospect, this check had not read any project-name variables in the template, nor had it saved the original input and hook-written value side by side.

This attempt did not prove that there was a problem with the tag branch, nor did it prove that the hook had not run. It only invalidated the old stopping condition: a directory change is not enough.

The failure was not in checking the directory itself. The directory should still be recorded because it is one result in the identity chain. The failure was allowing one result to stand in for the others. The revised approach is not to skip the directory, but to place the directory and the two variables side by side, allowing any one of them to temporarily have no observed value.

This review also left an edge case: `project-name` and `crate_name` may not come from the same source even if both appear in a “seemingly correct” format. One value may already reflect a hook write-back, while the other still retains interactive input; they just happen to both comply with their respective formatting rules. For samples like this, do not write “name is normal”; you must write down the value still visible at each position.

## Deprecated quick handling method

The old handling method had two steps: first check whether the directory was renamed; then, after the rename, check whether generation succeeded. If both conditions were met, it no longer checked the template variables or template content.

This method was indeed convenient when directories were easy to check and template content was difficult to identify, but now it should only be used for the initial observation. It is not suitable for making the final determination, for the following reasons:

1. A directory change cannot replace comparing `project-name` with `crate_name`;
2. Successful generation cannot replace comparing the Git template revision;
3. Passing in a selection option cannot replace verifying that the output content corresponds to the selected value;
4. A variable having a reasonable shape cannot replace verifying that the variable sources are consistent.

The old steps are not being removed so that people who arrive through old links understand why some records contain only the directory or only “tag passed.” These historical samples can continue to be used to locate the starting point, but they cannot be used directly to conclude the current investigation.

## Another track for template content

`generate` supports selecting, through `--tag`, the content corresponding to a specified tag in the Git template repository. Here, a common misreading must be avoided: the project directory name cannot prove which revision was selected. The directory is part of the target project, not a version marker for the template content.

The revision branch only needs to answer two questions: whether `--tag` was explicitly specified this time, and whether the generated result contains enough content to distinguish the template revision. If either answer is missing, do not write “looks like the old template” as a selection failure.

```text
Unexpected template content
│
├─ --tag not explicitly specified
│  └─ Do not attribute this to tag selection; retain the observation and leave this branch
│
├─ --tag specified, but the output contains nothing that distinguishes the revision
│  └─ Stop: the current sample cannot be used to compare tag content
│
├─ --tag specified, the output distinguishes the revision, and the content does not match
│  └─ Save the specified value and corresponding output, and check template source selection
│
└─ --tag specified, and the output content matches
   └─ End the revision branch; do not use it to explain identity variables
```

“Content that distinguishes the revision” must be template content actually visible after generation. The Git URL, directory timestamp, whether generation succeeded, and the default branch as remembered by the observer are not comparison material for this branch. If the output does not distinguish the revision, you can accurately write “cannot compare”; this does not call for additional template changes, but simply indicates that the current sample is insufficient to determine whether the selection was correct.

The old instructions said that supplying the tag parameter was enough to interpret subsequent content according to that tag. That statement is also marked **deprecated**. The parameter indicates the intended selection; only the output content shows whether this run's result matches that intent. Recording both prevents source selection and rendering anomalies from being conflated into a single judgment later.

## A parallel record, not a sequential checklist

Identity samples and revision samples should be kept separately. The former record how identity is used before and after the hook; the latter record the selection value and template content. This is not about making the table more complete, but about preventing the result of one branch from overriding the other.

Identity sample:

```text
Whether the init hook rename is confirmed:
Original input:
Value written by the hook:
Directory:
project-name:
crate_name:
Locations where the original input is still visible:
```

revision sample:

```text
Whether --tag was used:
Specified tag:
Content in the output that identifies the revision:
Whether that content matches the specified value:
Identity branch status:
```

The last line only reminds later readers not to merge the two samples. It is not meant to incorporate identity results into the revision conclusion. For example, even when the directory and variables are already consistent, the template content may still be unidentifiable; even when the output content already matches the selection value, the post-hook variables may still not have been checked.

If the evidence on one side is insufficient, stop that side. Do not fill the hook-rename sample with variables obtained during ordinary generation, or use a directory from another generation run to prove the content corresponding to this run's tag. Both ways of filling the gaps would leave subsequent review without a shared baseline from the same run.

## The distinction retained in the old meeting excerpt

Subsequent discussions retained a brief distinction: project identity and template revision do not follow the same decision tree.

On the project identity side, the question is whether the target directory and template variables still use the fallback value from the interactive phase after the init hook writes the name. `src/template_variables/project_name.rs` is the local reference point for checking format conversion; `ToKebabCase` and `ToSnakeCase` within it can help locate the different representations of the project name, but cannot replace verification of the actual references.

On the template revision side, the question is whether, after a selection value is specified, the template content ultimately rendered corresponds to that revision. This is not automatically true because the directory name changes, nor is it automatically true because a particular template variable is already correct.

This boundary only constrains how troubleshooting records are written; it does not assign ownership of the implementation. For samples where both sides show anomalies, it is best to save the observations from both sides together; if one side lacks evidence, leave only that side unknown rather than using the other side's result to fill in a conclusion.

## Two points that can still block the investigation

The first point is where the value written back by the hook enters the subsequent flow. `project_name.rs` provides a nearby reference for project-name conversion, but the current page does not identify it as the hook's implementation location. When checking back, first look at the object being formatted here, then follow the actual references to confirm whether the written-back value enters directory handling and variable construction.

The second point is the relationship between the template root and tag selection. The current page only requires comparing the selected revision against the output content; it does not fix their internal order. If the output has no distinguishable content, the revision branch remains unexamined by comparison; do not assume that the template root has already been determined in some particular order just to complete the flowchart.

These two unknowns cannot be merged. The former lacks the point where the value is obtained in the identity chain, while the latter lacks material for comparing template content. They can appear in the same review, but the next observation needed is different for each.

## 2025-07-18：Current criteria

The earlier rules, supplementary review notes, and failure reviews are retained to explain why the current checks no longer look only at the directory. Once a case is confirmed to involve renaming by the init hook, use the following requirement:

> The init hook may first write the raw project-name; the target directory must then be normalized to project-bar, and project-name and crate_name must be recalculated based on it, rather than continuing to use the interactive fallback name.

This requirement only addresses project identity. It does not specify which revision the Git template should select, and a passing tag branch cannot substitute for variable checks. The directory, `project-name`, and `crate_name` may each use an appropriate format; the requirement here is that they no longer continue to take the interactive fallback name after the hook renames the project.

When verifying on site, first obtain the original input and the value written by the hook. Then compare the actual directory with the visible variables. If the directory has changed but the original input is still visible in one or both variables, the identity branch is not complete. If the directory and both visible variables are all derived from the post-hook identity, the identity branch can be closed, even if the revision branch still requires a separate comparison. If the hook did not rename anything, this item does not draw a conclusion about the normal generation path.

When tracing back, still start with the area adjacent to the format conversion in `src/template_variables/project_name.rs`, then follow the actual references to confirm where the value written back enters the subsequent flow. Do not treat `heck::{ToKebabCase, ToSnakeCase}` as evidence for the entire generation flow; it can only narrow the scope for inspecting the representation of the project name.

## Old appendix: the former two-step quick check

The following two steps are still retained for people arriving from old links. They are not the current completion criteria.

1. Check whether the generated directory has been renamed; if it has, assume that the post-hook flow has fully adopted the new name.
2. Specify a tag and check whether generation succeeds; if it does, assume that the output comes from that tag.

The first step was invalidated by a review in which “the directory changed, but the variables were not compared.” The second step is also insufficient to show that the output content corresponds to the selected revision. They can serve as starting points for initial observations, but they cannot replace the five identity records and the template content comparison.

The old appendix has not been deleted because some historical cases left only a directory name and a note that “the tag was passed.” When dealing with these records, first acknowledge their scope: a directory change does not account for the variables, and the presence of an option does not account for the template content. Once the missing information has been added so that comparisons can be made within the same case, complete the identity and revision branches separately.

## Issues not yet split out

After the template source has been selected by tag, determining the template root and checking the project identity sometimes come up in the same review. The current page does not combine them into a “template anomaly.” If the revision cannot be identified from the output, retain the status that template content has not been compared; if the value written by the hook was not retained, retain the status that the identity source has not been confirmed. Both stopping conditions can exist at the same time.

# Rhai System Command Authorization Experiment Notes

This round brings the hook-related checks back to `tests/integration/hooks.rs`. The dependencies at the top of the file already show that these aren't notes on running a script in isolation: `indoc` keeps the template fragments, `OutputAssertExt` and `PredicateStrExt` are reserved for command-output assertions, and `binary` and `tmp_dir` prepare the project directory.

Two issues are mixed into this round. The first is the authorization boundary for system commands in Rhai; the second is how nested conditions behave when they receive boolean values. They share the hook test entry point, but a command-permission result must not be treated as coverage of conditional rendering. The conditional portion remains a pending counterexample in the same directory. Next time, we need to write out separately what content remains when the inner condition receives true and false.

This round observes operations in the generated project, rather than interpreting command locations relative to the test process's own directory. A template hook should reach system commands only after authorization; the unauthorized path should stop before command execution. The constraints here are: a Rhai hook may call system::command(program, arguments) only when the caller explicitly passes --allow-commands, the command's working directory is the generated project, and an execution failure must abort generation.

The checks therefore need to distinguish “template rendering completed” from “the hook succeeded.” The former only shows that the project directory and template content are in place; it does not establish the latter. If the hook fails, generation must not continue and return success. The existing output-assertion tools are sufficient for both observations; we won't split them into another set of helpers at this stage.

The additional nested-condition test changes only one variable: keep the same template and generated directory, and set the inner input to boolean true, then false. We need to confirm that the conditional branch is selected by value, rather than passing accidentally after treating the boolean as a string. If this additional test exposes a failure unrelated to command authorization, record it under the conditional item, not as an exception to the authorization rule.

# Configuration File and Working Directory Decision Record

This record originally tied two phenomena too closely together: the path taken when the default configuration file does not appear, and the directory in which the caller still remains after the library call ends. Both were placed in the 0.14 compatibility train, and early investigation of both also started around the generation entry point, so the draft used “generation completed normally” as their shared working language. That wording was convenient, but it conflated things that needed to be verified separately.

The draft did not classify them as the same implementation defect. The decision at the time was only to reject an easier acceptance approach: the fact that generation had finished could not be taken to mean that both configuration reading and the caller’s directory state were problem-free. Configuration reading concerns which branch is taken when input is missing; directory restoration concerns whether a library call leaves the process’s original current location intact. Both can occur at the same time, or only one of them can occur.

There were two options on the table at the time.

- Treat “the quiet path for the default configuration file” and “working-directory restoration after the library call” as one large regression, retaining only one result.
- Split them into two items: find the matching path through the discovery entry point on the configuration side, preserve state before and after the call on the directory side, and then determine whether they have a common cause.

The cost of the first approach was not merely shorter documentation; it made the results difficult to interpret. If a generation run completed, the reader would still not know whether it had skipped a configuration branch or whether the caller’s current directory had changed. If the directory changed, that could not be directly inferred to mean that configuration loading had failed. The draft chose the second approach, retaining two entry points and two open items; that choice remains valid.

## Starting Points Left by the Draft

The starting point on the configuration side is `src/app_config.rs`. This is not because the filename itself can provide a conclusion, but because the old investigation record led the reading here through terms such as configuration, loading, and file. The file header shows:

```rust
use anyhow::{Context, Result};
use console::style;
use serde::Deserialize;
use std::{
```

These lines do not tell us which return result the default configuration file will ultimately produce, nor do they list the configuration filename or search order. They only limit the early judgment to a small scope: the configuration module at least touches the error context, display style, and deserialization at the same time, so the default path cannot be handled solely as “read failed.” It was reasonable for the draft to stop here; there was not enough material at the time to turn the quiet path into a specific implementation commitment.

There is no corresponding source anchor on the directory side. Initially, some people tended to continue looking near the configuration module because the reading location might change during generation. That association was later retained as an old hypothesis rather than a basis for the decision. The caller’s current working directory is part of the state after the library call completes; even if configuration reading takes place in a particular directory, that does not establish whether the directory is or is not restored when the call ends.

Therefore, the draft’s statement that “both phenomena are near the generation entry point” was only a locating habit, not a causal judgment. Subsequent investigation no longer requires them to fall within the same function, file, or lifecycle segment. Keeping this old judgment in the record explains that the later split was not an ad hoc change of subject, but a narrowing of the original classification.

## Adjustments After the Cards Were Added

CG-206 later became the navigation entry point on the configuration side. It requires starting at the repository root, following the discovery process for “the quiet path for the default configuration file,” and retaining the final match list. The emphasis here is on starting at the repository root, not on first guessing that a particular configuration object is responsible for all the behavior. For this card, the current decision is to continue organizing the material around the paths actually matched; until there is a match list, do not expand the import or filename of `src/app_config.rs` into the complete rules for the default configuration file.

This also corrects an ambiguous statement in the draft. The draft treated “quiet” as a result that could already be accepted directly. The existing material does not provide the default configuration filename, search locations, priority, or the complete display content when the default file is encountered. “Quiet path” is now retained as historical terminology to identify the investigation target; it no longer independently represents a fixed error message or one unique return method.

CG-223 brought the other line back to the state after the library call. The card later gained a counterexample in subsequent records and moved from the backlog into active work. The specific counterexample is not written on this page and cannot replace the original comparison of directory states; however, it is sufficient to reject the simplified judgment that “if the lifecycle appears complete, there is no need to inspect the current directory.”

Later notes also confirmed only this segment of the generation lifecycle. Working-directory restoration after the library call still has one unconfirmed point, with its inputs and outputs retained in a temporary-repository state snapshot. This boundary is important: what has been confirmed is a segment of the generation lifecycle, not that the caller’s directory has been restored. Previously writing the two together as “compatibility after generation completes” could make people think that the directory issue had also been closed out; they are now explicitly kept separate.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ConfigDiscovery
    ConfigDiscovery: Default configuration file discovery
    ConfigDiscovery --> ConfigHits: Final match list pending
    [*] --> CallerBefore
    CallerBefore: Directory state before the library call
    CallerBefore --> CallerAfter: Directory state after the library call pending verification
```

The two state tracks in the diagram only describe the verification order for the current record. The configuration track goes from the discovery entry point to the final match list; the directory track goes from the state before the call to the state after the call. They have no merge node here because the existing material has not yet connected them to the same cause.

## Judgments Not Adopted This Time

During review, we again compared the approach of “downgrading the directory issue to test-environment residue.” Its appeal was that the generation process itself already had a confirmed segment, while the temporary repository could make the directory observation look like an environmental difference. But adopting this judgment would first require proving that the directory had not been changed by the library call; the existing record specifically retains this point as unconfirmed. Therefore, the issue was not classified as environment residue.

Nor did we instead identify the default configuration file’s path as the cause of the directory change. The configuration path and current directory may be related during the same call, but this page contains no evidence connecting them through one-way causality. If it is later found that both are triggered by the same directory switch, they should be merged only after new evidence is added; “they are both related to paths” cannot substitute for that evidence.

Another abandoned formulation was to directly designate the configuration module as the owner of directory restoration. `src/app_config.rs` remains on this page because it is a readable entry point for the configuration issue; it does not automatically explain the completed state of the library call. The compatibility cost of handling it this way is small: investigation requires following one additional entry point, but it does not assign an unconfirmed process state to the wrong module.

## Current Decision

This page keeps these two requirements in the 0.14 compatibility train as parallel records rather than as conditions that prove one another.

1. Verify the quiet path for the default configuration file through the configuration discovery process. CG-206 is the navigation entry point for this line, and the final match list should determine the location of any subsequent change or regression.
2. Verify working-directory restoration after the library call through the states before and after the call. The temporary-repository state snapshot in CG-223 retains the inputs and outputs for this line; confirmation of the generation lifecycle cannot replace this step.
3. Until there is new direct material for both lines, do not upgrade “generation succeeded,” “the configuration module is readable,” or “the lifecycle has been confirmed” into a completion conclusion for the other line.

Keeping them parallel does not require the two items to use the same test set, nor does it require them to share the same code ownership. It only constrains the order of judgment: first explain configuration discovery and the caller’s directory state separately, then discuss whether they need to be handled together. This avoids a regression that leaves only the conclusion “normal overall” without answering which state was actually observed.

## Corrections to the Old Wording

The draft’s wording “generation completed normally” is no longer used as a basis for judgment. It is retained because it reflects the working assumption at the time; now, however, it can describe only a broad phenomenon. It cannot prove how the default configuration file was handled, nor can it prove that the caller’s directory remained unchanged after the library call returned.

The draft also placed `src/app_config.rs` too close to the overall entry point. A more accurate description is that it is a local module already identified during configuration investigation. The dependencies in the file header can help continue reading adjacent content related to the error context, display, and deserialization, but they should not be treated as a map of the entire generation process. Verification of directory restoration should still start from the state changes during the library call, rather than being inferred from this file’s name.

DOC-16 records an interface review involving no-VCS and paths containing spaces. It also involves paths, but it is not incorporated into the basis for this decision. The concerns here are the discovery path for the default configuration and the caller’s current directory when the library call ends; whether interface parameters are passed natively and whether VCS is initialized remain within their respective review scopes.

## Field Material Still to Be Added

The configuration side needs the final match list required by CG-206. Once the list is available, the matched locations and excluded paths should be recorded directly after this decision, rather than being summarized again as “configuration loading checked.” If the match results show that the default file never passed through `src/app_config.rs`, the error in this early location should be retained, and the reading starting point should be moved to the actual branch.

The directory side needs a reproducible before-and-after comparison for the call that can correspond to the state snapshot in CG-223. The current note already states that this area still contains unconfirmed items, so this record should not presuppose successful restoration, lack of restoration, or which layer changed the directory. What should be added is the state difference itself and where it appeared, not a guess about the temporary-repository environment.

The two lines can ultimately be shown in the same regression, but the display order will no longer be determined by whether generation completed. First list the locations actually traversed by configuration discovery, then list the directory states before and after the library call; only when both sets of records are present should they be discussed as having a common cause.
