# Duplicate Template Variable Records Incident Postmortem

adj-template-variables For a while, the current revision for two revisions was placed in the same entry. This wording came from the earliest incident observation, not from a later synthesized overview. The first thing observed was that project-name normalization differed from the old record; only later was it discovered that the template source selector could still work, while the comparison content had been redirected to a local-path template. Later still, the hook, template test command, generated target directory, and caller regression each left traces. They were different observations of the same anomalous event, but not enough to consolidate them into a confirmed root cause.

This page therefore retains three layers: what was first seen, how the comparison scope was narrowed along the way, and which issues still had not been proven after recovery. Later records cannot retroactively replace earlier judgments.

## The Initial Evidence

v1 contained only a few lines at the time. The first observed difference was that project-name normalization differed from the old record. The original entry `docs/adj-template-variables/incidents/template-variables-dependency boundary audit-two-version records were not merged.md` was retained, and further retries were stopped. That version assumed that overwriting could restore the state, but it did not answer why the template test command had changed.

These lines were not deleted later. They serve two purposes: preserving the bias in the initial judgment and preserving the missing timestamp from that time. “Missing timestamp: ____” remains because no evidence could fill this blank with a reliable point in time. Filling it in as T+00, T+07, or some other time would feed the later timeline back into the earliest record.

The early sketch showed only object relationships, not the complete execution order:

```text
two revisions
      |
      v
same entry ——> template source selector ——> expansion / hook ——> output project
   |                              |
   +------ current revision ----------+
```

The diagram above is not a call graph. It only indicates that the comparison point at the time might move among the entry, source selection, and output. The only objects actually recorded were the entry, source selector, expansion process, and output project. Commands, parameters, and execution order that were not recorded must not be inferred from the diagram.

At the time, someone put “project-name normalization” first because it was the most obvious surface difference from the old record. This working hypothesis was not completely disproved later: after the project name was overwritten by the init hook, the target directory might change and the template variables might be recalculated. But it never independently explained why two revisions were in the same entry, nor why a local-path template appeared in the comparison result.

## How the Event Was Observed

At T+00, `template-variables-dependency boundary audit-two-version records were not merged` first diverged from the original revision. The team first saved the entry version and raw input, without immediately running it again. Stopping retries was not a recovery action; it merely prevented a second result from overwriting the first comparable material.

T+07, the template source selector was still working normally. This result weakened the assessment that “the entry point had failed completely,” but did not explain why two revisions could still appear at the same entry point. The comparison therefore narrowed to the first point of change: whether the source selection had changed, and which template tree was used after selection. “Still working normally” here applies only to this observation; it does not extend to the subsequent expansion and output.

T+18, the comparison pointed to a local-path template. This result made the initial attribution to the project name incomplete. The project name might still affect the target directory, but it alone could not explain why the source had already resolved to a local path. The corresponding branch was redirected to the maintenance entry point, and speculation about adjacent projects was not recorded as a cause during the investigation.

T+31, the user path was restored. The restoration time was recorded separately; root-cause confirmation was not announced along with the restoration. The green output in the old records could only show that a particular result was usable, not that the two revisions had been merged, nor that the same input would produce the same result later. Usability after restoration and entry-point identity are two separate matters.

This timeline does not include specific commands, accounts, or run numbers, because the source material did not preserve them. Later reviews can use entry-point and object names to locate relevant records, but cannot fabricate a complete reproduction from the timeline.

## Why the initial attribution was weakened

The earliest record focused on project-name normalization. This was not without basis: after the project name is overridden by the init hook, the target directory changes, and template variables may also be recalculated. However, the later investigation found a local-path template, a pre hook, and a post hook together, indicating that there were at least several adjacent steps from source selection to completed expansion. Attributing all of them to the project name would obscure the boundaries that actually needed comparison.

v2 added the observation that “the template source selector was still working normally.” It did not prove that the source selection result was correct, only that the selector had completed successfully at least once. The local-path template that appeared next did not prove that this branch was the sole cause either. Taken together, these two observations were enough to reject the claim that “the entry-point name alone can explain all the changes,” but not enough to replace it with another definitive attribution.

Another premature judgment was to treat the “change in the test command” as a consequence of changes to template content. The available records can only establish that the two versions of the records describe the template test command differently. They cannot establish that the command was executed during every generation, or that it rewrote the output. This remains unconfirmed and should not be presented as an outcome in the postmortem.

The output order also led to a misreading. During the investigation, green output appeared near the completion of expansion, and someone took it to mean that the entire process had finished. A later note distinguished the progress boundary from the post hook: if the post hook runs only after the progress boundary, looking only at the preceding output line will miss subsequent results. This observation explains why a retelling based on a screenshot was insufficient, but does not prove that the post hook caused revisions to be mixed.

Liquid expansion, template configuration, and placeholder values also cannot be assembled into a causal chain. They appear at different points in the review; among them, `placeholder value` indicates that a variable did not receive the expected substitution, but has no corresponding input or expansion stage. The current material does not allow the unsubstituted value to be traced to the project name, a revision, or any hook.

## Comparisons preserved in the intermediate version

v2 added a short timeline and also mapped out the source branches. It did not attribute all differences to the same cause. The table below preserves the comparison points used at the time, not a checklist designed later.

| Comparison point | Result preserved from the incident | What it can show | What it cannot show |
|---|---|---|---|
| Entry point | Two revisions were present in the same place | The comparison point was unstable | Cannot show which revision should be the current version |
| Source selector | Still working normally at T+07 | At least one part of the selection flow after the entry point was usable | Cannot show that the selected tree was necessarily correct |
| Local path template | Appeared in the comparison results at T+18 | This branch entered the local path template | Cannot prove that the path branch was the sole root cause |
| Project name normalization | Inconsistent with the old records | The target directory and variables may have been recalculated | Cannot explain the source change on its own |
| hook | pre hook and post hook were observed in sequence | The expansion process included pre- and post-actions | Cannot infer successful execution from the output order |
| Template test command | Notation differed between the two versions | Test-related behavior needs to be checked again | Cannot confirm the result without execution records |
| sub-template root | Listed as an adjacent selection point | The selected subtemplate may determine the template tree | Cannot show that it caused the mixing at the entry point |
| placeholder value | Appeared during the review of the expansion | A variable did not receive the expected value | Cannot trace it to a specific input or stage |

The asymmetry in the table needs to be preserved. The source selector had one incident observation of “still working normally,” while the local path template was only implicated by the comparison, without complete success and failure samples. The hooks were observed in sequence, but there were no execution returns for each step. The template test command had only a difference in notation, with no run results. Filling these columns to the same level of completeness would fabricate evidence that does not exist.

That screenshot-only retelling was later compared against the original entry point. A screenshot can preserve a line of output, but not the revision, input location, or surrounding relationships, so it cannot explain why another path worked normally. Preserving the original entry-point version is more useful than reorganizing the screenshots; the green status after reorganization cannot override the original incident evidence.

## Sources, template roots, and output locations

The focus of the review later shifted from “did the project name change” to “which template tree was actually selected.” When sub-template is configured, first confirm whether the selected subtemplate is the template root, rather than assuming the parent template tree is the output source. This judgment only constrains the order of comparison; it is not a fix already completed for this incident.

The local path template appeared in the comparison results at T+18. This shows that at least one input path entered the local path template at the time. It does not tell us which revision selected that path, nor why the entry-point records retained both versions at once. The incident review can retain this branch without treating “local path” as a universal answer.

Changes to the target directory caused by overriding the project name must also be saved separately. If the init hook changes the project name to another value, the old directory and the normalized directory cannot be combined and described as a single output location. Template variables may be recalculated based on the target location, and a `placeholder value` may appear at one of the stages, but the existing records do not connect these two phenomena.

This is also why v2 included “working directory restoration” and “generation target directory” in the review scope. They are adjacent boundaries between the output location and the invocation environment, not confirmation of the root cause. Without actual directory records, we can only retain the direction of comparison; we cannot fill in directory names or execution commands.

## Hooks and output order

Early screenshots treated a line of green output near the completion of expansion as the endpoint. Later notes showed that the pre hook and post hook appeared separately in the records, so the progress boundary cannot automatically mean that all subsequent actions have finished. The review therefore needs to distinguish three points: the end marker for the expansion process, where the progress boundary appears, and whether post hook output is still visible afterward.

This distinction only addresses “which section of output to look at.” It does not mean that the post hook definitely ran, that the post hook modified the template content, or, still less, that it changed the revision selection. If only screenshots from before the progress boundary are available, the post hook's status remains unknown.

Likewise, whether the template test command ran cannot be inferred from the appearance of the word “test” on the page. v2 retained it as a suspected change because the descriptions in the two versions of the records were inconsistent; v3 continues to retain this gap because no new execution records have been added. Offline build evidence and caller regression testing can also only be treated as unfinished follow-up material, not as proof of the recovery scope.

## Recovery actions did not extend to reworking the setup

Three concrete things were done during recovery: the original entry-point version was saved, further overwriting was stopped, and the overwrite-write path that was already working was restored. The sole purpose was to restore the user path and preserve the original for comparison. Recovery did not clear the two old revisions, nor did it turn the current entry point into a new long-term entry point.

The statement “overwrite writing can restore functionality” remains in the old paragraph, but it only represents a single recovery observation made at the time. It does not specify which target location was overwritten or whether the same revision was still used after recovery. Elevating it to a general rule would go beyond the material left by this incident.

No confirmation of the root cause was announced after recovery was complete. Making the user path usable only resolved the usage blocker at the time; object version identifiers, separation of objects with the same name, branching after the current entry point, and single-variable reruns remained unresolved. The old records continue to be cited because they preserve the chronology of the first deviation and the reasons for stopping retries, not because they have become a new unified operations page.

If two revisions appear at the entry point again, the on-site sequence should still be to save the original, stop overwriting, and then check the source selector. If the source selector is still working normally, continue comparing the selected template tree; if the result enters the local-path template branch, record that branch and the revision at the time. If only the green output before the progress boundary is visible, do not treat it as evidence that the post hook has completed. Even after the user path is restored, retain the pre-recovery results.

## Object identity and subsequent entry points

The archived records for CGC-001 identify `template-variables-supply-boundary` as an object with the same name whose version needs to be clearly labeled. This addresses the risk of confusing referenced objects, not the root cause of this incident. After separating the two objects with the same name, each object's corresponding revision and entry point version still need to be kept alongside the original record.

CGC-017 later confirmed that the object was available and handed off the forks beyond the current entry point to the maintainer for further handling. What can be confirmed here is that the object already has a usable entry point; this card does not establish which revision was used in this incident or when the old entry point was retired.

The record for CGC-018 preserves the approach of tracing from the execution record to the first broken link and stopping at the result as it stood then. It changed the focus of the review: the first broken link preserves the incident state better than the final line of green output. The record did not retroactively mark the portion before the broken link as successful, nor did it treat the portion after the stopping point as already completed.

The rerun approach for CGC-019 is to keep `template-variables-supply-boundary`, the current entry point, and the command fixed, replacing only the current revision. This matches the scope of the anomaly on this page exactly, but this page contains no rerun results. This action remains a comparison yet to be completed, not a validation conclusion.

The related cards are used only to locate objects and subsequent entry points. They cannot replace the sequence of events on this page, nor can they fill in the maintainer, version forks, or exit conditions as matters already decided.

## Scope of impact

The impact primarily affects template consumers using this entry point: the same entry point cannot consistently represent a single revision, so consumers may receive templates from different sources. The comparison path pointed to a local-path template at one point, indicating that the impact was not merely a change to the page name. A project name change may also change the target directory and template variables, so recovery cannot consist solely of replacing the entry point text.

The scope of impact has not been extended to adjacent services. There is no evidence in the records that adjacent projects experienced the same mixing of revisions, nor is there evidence that all templates were affected. The wording here is “consumers using this entry point”; unlisted consumers are not described as affected.

Caller-side regression testing was included in the subsequent list of differences, but there are no corresponding pass or fail results. At present, this only indicates that the entry point's behavior needs to be reviewed again from the caller's side; it does not indicate that callers have recovered. Evidence for offline builds is likewise still incomplete and cannot be replaced by green output.

Changes to the template test command, changes to the generated target directory, and the appearance of placeholder values may all affect consumers' assessment at the same time, but the available material does not establish that they occurred together in the same run. This postmortem retains these observations to preserve starting points for later review, not to assemble them into a single failure chain.

## Why the old account is still retained

An old record once said, “Overwriting can restore it.” This statement was useful during that recovery, but it did not specify which target location was overwritten, nor whether the same revision was still used after recovery. Keep this statement now, while limiting it to a recovery observation.

The old record also put “project name normalization” first. After it was later discovered that the source selector was still functioning normally, this conclusion was weakened, but it was not erased from the historical paragraphs. It represents the earliest working hypothesis available at the time. If readers look only at the latest paragraph, they will mistakenly believe that the relationship between the entry point, source, and hook was known from the beginning; that does not match the actual record.

Another piece of old text left “it is still unknown why the template test command changed” as a gap. This gap still exists. Even though later observations were added about the template configuration and Liquid expansion, they do not justify filling in the difference in the test command as having already been executed or already failed.

“the current revision of two revisions is placed at the same entry point” must not be polished into a more precise version-selection conclusion. The existing material supports only that the entry point simultaneously carries two version identifiers; it cannot indicate which version was supposed to overwrite which version, nor whether the mixing occurred during saving, selection, or expansion.

The old accompanying records also retained the terms “favorite entry,” “offline build evidence,” and “caller regression.” They are not evidence of the same strength: the first is merely a place to look back at, while the latter two are incomplete materials. Changing them all into completed checks would destroy the historical state of this page.

## Boundaries of follow-up review

Starting from `template-variables-supply-boundary`, the two revisions can be saved separately, with the current entry point and command held fixed and only the revision replaced. Each comparison must retain the source selector result, whether the local path template was selected, the target directory after project name normalization, the placeholder value, and the output locations of the pre hook and post hook. This can show which variable changed and was followed by a change in the behavior, but it cannot directly label a single difference as the root cause.

If two revisions appear again at the entry point during the follow-up review, first save the original and stop overwriting. If the source selector is still functioning normally, continue comparing the selected template tree; if the result enters the local path template, record that path and the revision at the time. If only green output before the progress boundary is visible, do not treat it as meaning that the post hook has completed. If the user path has already been restored, still retain the result from before the recovery.

If the target directory changes because of project-name overwriting, save the old directory and the normalized directory separately; do not merge the two locations into a single “output directory.” If a template variable shows a placeholder value, record which expansion stage it appeared in; there is currently no material proving that it definitely came from the project name, nor any material proving that it definitely came from the revision.

If sub-template is configured, first save the root of the selected child template, then compare it separately with the parent template tree and the local path template. Do not infer the template root from the final output alone, because the same output may be affected simultaneously by the project name, source selection, and hooks. This branch can only help identify the comparison objects; it cannot close the incident on its own.

If pre hook or post hook is recorded again, save the output both before and after the progress boundary. When there is only green output for the preceding segment, whether the post hook ran remains unknown; when only subsequent output appears, that still cannot be used to infer that the preceding expansion definitely used the expected revision. Output order and version identity need to be recorded separately.

Offline build evidence is still incomplete. Caller regression appears only in the subsequent difference list, with no corresponding pass or fail result. Both can continue to be investigated, but neither can be used to fill in the scope of successful recovery.

## Changes Retained Between Versions

v1 only established that the entry had two revisions, that project-name normalization differed from the old record, and that overwritten writes could be recovered; changes to the template test command were unknown. It had no timeline and did not separate the source selector from the local path template.

v2 added four relative time points, T+00, T+07, T+18, and T+31, confirmed that the template source selector had remained operational, and also confirmed once that the result pointed to a local path template. It documented the problem that the screenshot paraphrase lacked the original input, and separated recovery from root-cause confirmation. Template configuration, Liquid expansion, the hook, the generation target directory, and working-directory restoration were listed as adjacent observations.

v3 did not remove v2's conclusions. Instead, it placed the pre hook, post hook, placeholder value, sub-template root, progress boundary, caller regression, and offline build evidence back in their respective evidence locations. They appear in parallel; this does not mean these observations were all confirmed in a single run.

v3 also handled source selection and output location separately. Whether the entry simultaneously carries two revisions is an object identity issue; whether the template source selector can still complete its flow is a selection-flow issue; and the local path template, target directory, and placeholder value are output-side observations. Putting all three in one paragraph can show that they are adjacent, but adjacency must not be written as causality.

The final working judgment retained is: restoring the user path does not equal confirming the revision boundary, and confirming that the object is usable does not equal determining when the old entry exited service. The current entry can still be used to locate the old incident state, but the adoption scope, maintenance entry point, and exit conditions for the two revisions have not yet been consolidated here into a new unified position.

## Still Open

- How to mark the revisions separately for the two objects with the same name in `template-variables-supply-boundary`.
- Who will continue maintaining the forks downstream of the current entry point, and when to retire the old entry point.
- After fixing the entry point, command, and template boundaries, replace only the rerun results for the current revision.
- Whether the template test command actually ran in this path, and whether it affected the output.
- The selection order among the sub-template root, the parent template tree, and the local path template.
- Whether the post hook produced output after the progress boundary that was missed in the screenshot.
- The actual changes to the target directory and placeholder values after project name normalization.
- Evidence from caller regression testing and offline builds.

These items cannot automatically be marked complete just because the user path has been restored. The old entry point and old version are still retained so that the next comparison can start from the same state, rather than hiding unanswered questions behind a recovery result that looks normal.

# On-Call Runbook for a Failed Dependency-Boundary Run

## Entry

This page covers only one actual run of `template-variables-supply-boundary`. First confirm that the on-call target still belongs to `adj-template-variables`, then open the record from `docs/adj-template-variables/runbooks/template-variables-dependency-boundary-audit-on-call-page-for-one-failed-run.md`. Do not attach output from another run to this page, and do not replace the live record with a conclusion before starting.

Before starting, record three things: the complete command used for this run, the template source actually reached, and the generated target directory. If the command or source code needs to change, save the pre-change content first; the decisions on this page depend on the objects seen at runtime and cannot be based only on directory names or default values. If the entry file does not match the live state, stop at the entry, record the paths and objects seen, and hand it back to the entry's maintainer.

## Live Sequence

1. **Find the local landing point first.** In the on-call page above, search for “crate-name derivation.” Continue downward only through the record in that section; do not combine template-variable descriptions from other projects. If that section cannot be found, stop the run. Do not guess whether the variable comes from a parent template, child template, or generated target directory.

2. **Save the first failure.** From the start of the run, check the output in the order visible on site. As soon as a failure, missing file, path change, or missing expected state first appears, immediately copy that segment of the raw output and write down the object it corresponds to beside it. Do not clean up the directory, rerun multiple parameter sets, or skip the first failure to inspect the later “caller regression.” Later output may be attached to the same record, but it must not overwrite the first failure.

3. **When you reach the progress boundary.** Do not clean up the live state after seeing “progress boundary.” It only shows that the run reached that point; by itself, it cannot prove that the template source, variable value, or target directory is correct. Keep the output from before and after the boundary, marking separately the last object seen and the first object that did not appear next. If the two cannot be distinguished, leave the unknown item as-is.

4. **Assess the caller regression.** If “caller regression” does not appear, stop here and do not write a success conclusion. Record it as a subsequent observation only if the marker actually appears in the live run. Even if it appears later, retain the earlier first failure and progress boundary; the regression marker must not cancel out the earlier anomaly.

5. **Change one condition at a time.** When a recheck is needed, first hold the source code, entry, and all other command parameters constant, changing only one explicitly recorded condition. Write the result of each recheck on its own line, stating what changed, the first visible change, and whether it stopped at the same step again. Leave combinations that were not actually observed blank; do not use results from an adjacent run as evidence for this run.

## Stop and Roll Back

Stop if any of the following occurs: “crate-name derivation” cannot be found; the first failure's object or raw output was not saved; continuing after the “progress boundary” requires cleaning up the live state; “caller regression” has not appeared but someone is preparing to write a success result; or the current entry does not match the record in the file. When stopping, do not broaden the investigation or rewrite the live state just to obtain a complete path.

Rollback is limited to known restoration actions: retain the old entry, restore the source code and command record from before the change, do not delete failure output, and do not write an unverified restoration action as completed. The restoration action has not yet been tried in the shared environment, so the state in the shared environment cannot serve as a successful sample for this page. If the object still cannot be confirmed after rollback, stop at the last visible step.

## Handoff Record

Write the handoff content beside the corresponding steps on this page in the following order:

- The entry used: `docs/adj-template-variables/runbooks/template-variables-dependency-boundary-audit-on-call-page-for-one-failed-run.md`;
- The raw output for the first failure and the object it corresponds to;
- The last output segment retained before and after the “progress boundary”;
- Whether “caller regression” appeared;
- The single condition changed, the exit code, and the state still visible after rollback;
- The specific step the next shift should continue from and which combinations remain unverified.

If the record reaches only the first failure, stop the handoff at the first failure; if it reaches only the progress boundary, hand off only through the progress boundary. Do not write the “template source selector,” generated target directory, or sub-template root as confirmed causes unless the raw output from this run actually connects them to the failed object. This on-call page and its attachments are still maintained by `adj-template-variables`; open a new version for subsequent changes rather than overwriting the live record for this run.

# Public Entry Maintenance Decision Record

The record for 6 month began with a very narrow dispute: whether the team's public entry should switch directly to the new location during the adjustment window. The meeting did not treat “the entry is still accessible” as proof that the migration had succeeded, nor did it write the expected benefits of the new location as results that had already occurred. The final decision was to retain the current configuration entry for now. This decision addressed the switching risk at the time; it was not a long-term endorsement of the old entry.

## The Two Options on the Table at the Time

Continuing to use the current entry had the most direct benefit of not requiring the team to immediately change its familiar access method, while existing handoff materials could still be found in their original location. The maintenance cost would continue to exist: the old wording would not disappear automatically just because it remained reachable, and people taking over later might read a piece of historical documentation as a complete current description. The review kept this cost in the decision rather than erasing it with the word “stable.”

The other option was to switch to the new location during the adjustment window and then organize the entry and handoff materials centrally. Its benefit was only a plan awaiting validation: the materials might be more centralized, and the handoff might be easier to find. The switch itself would also introduce new variables. Callers would need to reconfirm where to enter, what input was actually provided, and when the first result appeared. The meeting had no evidence that the old and new entries carried the same input, nor evidence that the first visible result after the switch would remain unchanged.

Therefore, “switch as soon as the window begins” was not approved. The window could provide time for centralized handling, but it could not by itself become a condition for taking the old entry offline. If the old entry were removed first and a call later failed, the access path, handoff process, and generation flow would all enter investigation at the same time, making it difficult on site to determine where the deviation began. The current entry was retained so that these layers of impact could still be examined separately; this did not classify the new location as infeasible.

## Order of the Review Records

The addendum for 10 month changed the order of recording. First record whether people can enter through the public entry, then the input actually provided by the caller, and finally the first visible result just displayed by the command or call. These three cannot be combined into a single statement that “the path did not change.” Entry reachability answers only the access layer and cannot attest to the input content; input that appears identical cannot attest to subsequent results either.

The first result especially cannot be retained only when it is successful. It may be a prompt that appears when the generation flow starts, or it may be a failure that occurs very early. If the change appears after the entry handoff but before the call has started, it should continue to be recorded at the entry site; if the input has already been obtained and the call subsequently fails at cargo-generate, the record should remain at the call site. Both situations may look like “nothing was generated,” but they require returning to different places for review.

The successful path is saved separately. If the caller enters through the current entry and sees the generation flow start, that only shows that the old landing point worked up to this step. It does not show that the new entry is ready to take over, nor that later generation results will have no differences. If a later result deviates, continue recording it against that call rather than treating the continued accessibility of the entry as proof of success.

Adjacent failures are also saved separately. When a person cannot obtain content at the entry, first retain the access or handoff phenomenon rather than immediately writing it up as a generation failure; when the input has already been obtained and the failure occurs at cargo-generate, the failure still belongs to the call site. If the first result changes immediately after replacing the entry, stop the switch at that point and reproduce it through the old entry. Temporarily retaining both paths makes it easier to see where the change occurred than compressing the two layers of phenomena into one conclusion.

## Actual Impact Retained by the Decision

The direct impact of continuing to use the current entry is that a familiar public landing point for the team remains available during the adjustment. The coordinator can review the input and first result again from the same location, and the handoff does not have to handle entry replacement and call differences at the same time. The cost is equally clear: the historical wording and new explanations will coexist for a period, and the old materials may still be misread. This arrangement was therefore not written up as “the problem has been solved.”

The expected benefit of switching to the new location was to organize the entry and handoff materials centrally and reduce dependence on the old landing point. The review did not treat the expectation as an actual benefit, because at the time no real call could prove that the new location changed the call result, and it had not been confirmed that all callers were ready. The adjustment window can still be used to check these differences, but the date itself does not change the decision.

The discussion repeatedly returned to three specific facts from thepresentfield: where people enter, what input the call carries, and when the first result changes. If entry access is normal but the input record is missing, that cannot be used to approve the switch; if the input is identical but the first result differs, it also cannot be explained simply by saying “the entry did not change.” The statement “the path did not change” in the old record was too broad; the addendum for 10 month only broke it down and did not claim that all subsequent impacts had been investigated.

The meeting materials required the actual impact, the coordinator, and a reversible old entry to be recorded. The coordinator currently confirmed is Chen Siyuan. Long-term ownership, a unified switch date, and the migration status of all callers, where unsupported by the materials, have still not been written as facts. People participating in the review may add the call or handoff materials they actually obtained, but that will not automatically change the subject of this round's decision.

## Retained Earlier Opinions

“Switch during the window first, then organize the entry centrally” remains in the old record. It expresses a preference for centralized handling, not an already approved switching step. If this sentence were rewritten as the current process, readers would assume that the new location, input, and first result had already been confirmed to correspond directly. Its original tendency is retained here, with the unresolved on-site issues noted beside it.

The objection that keeping the old entry available will extend the period during which historical wording coexists has also not been deleted. It cannot be offset by calling it a “stable landing point,” nor will it disappear automatically because the adjustment window has begun. New content should be placed in the handoff record, while the old entry continues to serve review and rollback purposes; this decision did not expand the old documentation into a new complete guide.

Earlier materials also left a broader judgment: the entry did not change, and therefore the call path did not change. That judgment was sufficient at the time to support postponing the switch, but it was narrowed in the 10 month review. The entry, input, and first result may each change independently, so the entry status can no longer represent the entire call path. The old judgment is retained to explain why the switch was not made immediately at the time; the narrowed record explains that it now covers only the entry layer.

## Diagram and On-Site Usage

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Current configuration entry] --> B[Caller input]
  B --> C[First visible result]
  D[Adjustment window] --> E[New location]
  E --> B
  A --> F[Reversible old entry]
```

The order in the diagram is the recording method adopted for subsequent reviews, not a process that had already been clearly written in 6 month. The diagram places the adjustment window before the new location to show that the window provides an opportunity for handling; it does not mean that switching is mandatory when the time arrives. The old entry points to a reversible landing point, which does not mean that two sets of entries must always be maintained simultaneously; it indicates that there is still an option to return to the original location if the switch fails.

If a review obtains only a result showing that entry access is normal, it can be recorded only in the entry box. Without the corresponding input and first result, it cannot be upgraded to approval for the switch. If the result obtained is an adjacent failure at the entry, first retain the old entry and record where it occurred; if it is a failure after the input has been handed to cargo-generate, continue checking it at the call site. The record may temporarily look untidy this way, but failures from different locations will not be mixed together.

If the default landing point is to be reevaluated later, it must at least be possible to correlate the entry, input, and first result to the same call, and the switch must still be reversible. Here, “reversible” means that the old entry has not been discarded first; it is not an abstract long-term commitment. The current materials provide neither a unified switch date nor evidence that all callers have completed migration, so this version does not add either item.

## Decision in This Version

The current configuration entry will continue as the team's public landing point, the adjustment window will not trigger an automatic switch, and the old entry will be retained as a rollback point. Maintenance records begin with a real cargo-generate call and describe the entry, input, and first visible result separately; entry reachability does not substitute for generation success, and a failure during generation is not written back as an entry failure.

This decision did not change the call semantics of cargo-generate, nor did it approve new long-term ownership of the entry. For handoff continuity after entry replacement, see also DOC-44. If the next review still has only the entry status and lacks the input and first result from the same call, this record remains at the decision to retain the current entry.

# Public Entry Point Maintenance Walkthrough

The first version recorded `src/template.rs` and `template-rendering`, then stopped at the direct caller soon afterward. The review showed that listing every file containing template or rendering wasn't what helped. What helped was placing this entry point back in the “Team Public Entry Point Maintenance” collaboration context and identifying the first actual consumer it reached there. The path is still narrow, but it now has one more traceable relationship than the first version.

```text
src/template.rs
    │
    └─ template-rendering
          │
          └─ Repository public entry point
                │
                └─ Direct caller
                      │
                      └─ Team Public Entry Point Maintenance
                            │
                            └─ First actual consumer
```

### What the starting point establishes

`src/template.rs` is the file anchor for this trace. `template-rendering` corresponds to the repository's public entry point here. Start by looking outward from this location rather than guessing which module it belongs to from the filename. The filename helps establish a search starting point; the entry point and its next hop determine whether to keep following the path.

The same-named location does not automatically become a second entry point. The review record does not contain enough call relationships to connect it to this path, so it serves only as a signpost: it can help check whether the trace has gone off course, but cannot supply a parent-child relationship. Other template-related locations are not being assembled into a “complete template chain,” either. That would mistake search hits for call relationships.

# Shared Entry-Point Maintenance Deviation Postmortem

This deviation occurred during a maintenance window for the team's shared entry point. When the window ended, the entry was still visible, but the result visitors saw did not match the original plan. The on-site record first separated “entry accessible” from “maintenance result correct”; at that point, the only impact that could be confirmed was to the visible content of the shared entry point. Whether the generation command or other projects were affected was not confirmed then.

## Incident timeline

- During the maintenance window: The shared entry point was handled according to the original plan, but the process record was incomplete.
- First discovered: The check result did not match expectations. Further changes were paused, and the CLI output on the on-call terminal was retained.
- Temporary response: The entry was restored to an accessible state. The restoration occurred within the window, but there is no minute-level timestamp and no evidence that the root cause had been identified.
- During the postmortem: Gao Yan helped organize the impact and coordination details, while Zheng Wei preserved the anomaly observed on site. They treated “maintenance completed” and “result verified” as two separate states.

The raw output excerpt retained at the time under CLI is below; the original terminal text was not fully backfilled:

> CLI Raw output excerpt: `The visible result did not match the original plan`

This excerpt proves only that the deviation was seen on site; it does not prove where the divergence occurred. The initial assessment was that this was a display discrepancy during the maintenance window. Later material was still insufficient to confirm or overturn that assessment, so the earlier wording is retained here rather than being written as an attribution to a specific component. The affected entry's access method, the order of the maintenance actions, and the actual content displayed before and after restoration were not saved item by item at the time.

## Controls retained in the postmortem

The record was supplemented with three things that had been documented too vaguely during the shift: the actual impact, the coordinator, and the old entry that could be rolled back. The old entry was not deleted after the temporary restoration; it remained as a rollback option. In the next similar window, first verify what visitors actually see, then decide whether to roll back or continue adjusting; “restored” alone is not enough to judge that maintenance is complete.

Still unconfirmed: exactly which action caused the divergence between the original plan and the final display; whether the CLI output corresponds to the entry itself or the result returned after maintenance; and whether the temporary restoration changed the preconditions for a subsequent window. Until these records exist, do not attribute this incident to a specific component or treat a single temporary restoration as a permanent fix.

Addendum: During the next window, the on-call person will save a screenshot of the entry and the original command text at the same time, for comparison between the two states.

# Shared Entry Point Maintenance Results Troubleshooting Tree

A ticket says “team shared entry point maintenance” is complete, but the results still can't be verified. First ask for the call entry point and version for `template-rendering`.

```text
Ticket marked complete
└─ Entry point and version?
   ├─ Either missing: stop; find someone who can confirm
   └─ Both available: compare paired call records for the same input
      ├─ Mismatch: stop at the difference; record the actual impact
      └─ Match but results differ: confirm the coordinator and whether the old entry point can be withdrawn
```

Who takes over when the two sides don't match has not been documented yet.
